items.explanation: The Dawes Act allotted reservations in individual parcels, but any land left over was declared 'surplus' and opened to white purchase. Between this mechanism and subsequent sales, tribes lost roughly 90 million acres — about two-thirds of their 1887 land base — showing how the assimilationist policy simultaneously fed settler demand for land.
options: (A) The law's primary purpose was to restore to tribes lands that had been seized through earlier fraudulent treaties.
(B) The law guaranteed that all reservation land would remain permanently under tribal ownership.
(C) The law functioned mainly as a federal jobs program for unemployed Native workers.
(D) The law's assimilationist design also served white land hunger: after allotments were made, remaining reservation land was sold to white settlers, costing tribes some 90 million acres.
items.stem: The 'surplus' land provision of the Dawes Act best illustrates which of the following?
items.stimulus: "...the President of the United States [is] hereby... authorized, whenever in his opinion any reservation or any part thereof of such Indians is advantageous for agricultural and grazing purposes, to cause said reservation... to be surveyed... and to allot the lands in said reservation in severalty [separate plots of land, individually owned] to any Indian located thereon..." — Dawes Severalty Act (excerpt), 1887

option_explanations.A: This is the opposite of what the provision did. The Dawes Act did not restore lands lost to fraudulent treaties — it broke up the reservations that remained. The 'surplus' mechanism took reservation land after allotments were assigned and sold it to white settlers, shrinking tribal holdings rather than returning stolen ones.
option_explanations.B: The law did the reverse of guaranteeing permanent tribal ownership. By allotting reservations in individual parcels — and then declaring everything left over 'surplus' — it dissolved the tribal land base itself. Tribal ownership was what the Act was designed to end, not protect.
option_explanations.C: The Dawes Act was not a jobs program. It was a land-allotment and assimilation law: its machinery was surveying, allotment in severalty, and the sale of 'surplus' land. Employment of Native workers was not its purpose or its mechanism.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The allotment process worked like this: each reservation was surveyed and divided into individual parcels, and whatever remained after every family received its allotment was declared 'surplus' and opened to white purchase. Through this mechanism — plus later sales of allotted land — tribes lost roughly 90 million acres, about two-thirds of their 1887 land base. The 'surplus' provision shows how the assimilationist design simultaneously satisfied white land hunger.

items.explanation: Jackson's A Century of Dishonor (1881) documented federal betrayals of treaties; she mailed a copy to every member of Congress. The moral pressure from such 'friends of the Indian' reformers helped produce the allotment policy.
options: (A) The Supreme Court's ruling in Worcester v. Georgia.
(B) A mass nonviolent protest movement against federal policy led by Crazy Horse.
(C) The Freedmen's Bureau's record of aiding formerly enslaved people in the South.
(D) Helen Hunt Jackson's A Century of Dishonor exposed federal mistreatment.
items.stem: An important impetus for the Dawes Act was which of the following?

option_explanations.A: Worcester v. Georgia (1832) belongs to a different era and a different fight — the Marshall Court's defense of Cherokee sovereignty against Georgia, half a century before allotment. It was about tribal nationhood, not the 1880s campaign to break up reservations.
option_explanations.B: Crazy Horse was a Lakota military leader of armed resistance (Little Bighorn, 1876; killed 1877), not the head of a nonviolent protest movement — and armed Plains resistance hardened opinion against Native peoples rather than inspiring the reformers who pushed allotment. The impetus for the Dawes Act came from eastern 'friends of the Indian' reformers, not from the battlefield.
option_explanations.C: The Freedmen's Bureau aided formerly enslaved people in the postwar South — a different population, a different region, a different policy world. It had no role in shaping federal Indian land policy in the 1880s.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Helen Hunt Jackson's A Century of Dishonor (1881) documented a century of broken federal treaties with Native nations, and she mailed a copy to every member of Congress. The moral pressure from Jackson and the 'friends of the Indian' reformers — who believed allotment would 'civilize' Native peoples by making them individual landowners — was an important impetus behind the Dawes Act of 1887.

items.explanation: Off-reservation boarding schools (e.g., Carlisle) cut children's hair, banned Native languages, imposed English names and vocational training — the same assimilationist logic as allotment: erase tribal identity by remaking the individual. The Indian Reorganization Act (1934) reversed this; AIM (1968) opposed it.
options: (A) The Ghost Dance movement's spiritual revival.
(B) The federal Indian boarding schools that erased Native languages.
(C) The Indian Reorganization Act's restoration of tribal governments.
(D) The American Indian Movement's 1960s activism.
items.stem: Which of the following shared the Dawes Act's underlying goal for the future of Native peoples?

option_explanations.A: The Ghost Dance was Native spiritual resistance to assimilation, not an expression of it. The 1890 movement promised the disappearance of whites and the return of the buffalo — a vision of deliverance from the very policies the Dawes Act embodied. It shared nothing with allotment's goal.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The off-reservation boarding schools — Carlisle being the famous example — pursued the same goal as allotment by different means: erase tribal identity by remaking the individual. Children had their hair cut, were forbidden to speak Native languages, were given English names, and were trained for manual labor. Allotment attacked tribalism through land; the schools attacked it through children. Both were instruments of forced assimilation.
option_explanations.C: The Indian Reorganization Act (1934) reversed the Dawes Act's goal, not shared it. The IRA ended allotment, restored the remaining land base, and encouraged tribal governments — the New Deal's repudiation of assimilation.
option_explanations.D: The American Indian Movement (founded 1968) opposed assimilationist policy, not continued it. AIM's activism — from the Trail of Broken Treaties to Wounded Knee — demanded treaty rights and tribal sovereignty, the opposite of the Dawes Act's program of dissolving tribes into individual landowners.

items.explanation: The 1873 cartoon shows a Granger waking figures sleeping on railroad 'sleepers' (ties) as a locomotive labeled 'Consolidation Train,' 'extortion,' and 'bribery' bears down — the Grange warning farmers that unregulated railroad corporations threatened their livelihoods and the republic itself.
options: (A) Railroads were bringing prosperity to formerly isolated farming communities.
(B) Railroad corporations were neglecting the safety of their own workers.
(C) Americans needed to wake up to the danger giant railroad monopolies posed.
(D) Rail lines were corrupting rural culture by importing urban vices.
items.stem: [Image description: 'The Grange Awakening the Sleepers,' 1873 political cartoon. Figures sleep on railroad tracks (the crossbeams are called 'sleepers') while a standing Granger tries to rouse them; a locomotive rushes toward them with cars labeled 'Consolidation Train,' 'extortion,' 'bribery,' and similar terms.] The cartoon's main point is which of the following?

option_explanations.A: The cartoon attacks the railroads; it does not celebrate them. The locomotive bearing down on the sleepers is labeled 'Consolidation Train,' 'extortion,' and 'bribery' — symbols of menace, not of prosperity brought to isolated farms.
option_explanations.B: Worker safety is not the cartoon's subject. The figures asleep on the tracks are farmers (the 'sleepers' pun is on railroad ties), and the danger rushing toward them is corporate monopoly power — extortionate rates and bribery — not unsafe working conditions for railroad employees.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The 1873 cartoon 'The Grange Awakening the Sleepers' puns on railroad ties ('sleepers') to show farmers asleep while a locomotive labeled 'Consolidation Train,' 'extortion,' and 'bribery' rushes at them. A standing Granger tries to rouse them. The message: farmers must wake up to the danger that unregulated railroad monopolies pose to their livelihoods — and the Grange is the alarm.
option_explanations.D: The cartoon says nothing about urban vices corrupting rural culture. Its targets are named on the train cars — consolidation, extortion, bribery — economic and political abuses by railroad corporations, not cultural contamination from the cities.

items.explanation: The National Grange of the Order of Patrons of Husbandry (founded 1867) organized farmers — first for mutual aid and better techniques, then for state railroad regulation (the Granger Laws) and cooperatives that bypassed middlemen.
options: (A) Farmers in the Midwest and West.
(B) Urban immigrant workers.
(C) Wealthy industrialists.
(D) Middle-class corporate managers.
items.stem: The Grange drew its strongest support from which group?

option_explanations.A: Correct. The National Grange of the Order of Patrons of Husbandry, founded in 1867, organized farmers — concentrated in the Midwest and West, where railroad dependence was greatest. It began with mutual aid and better farming techniques and grew into a political force for state railroad regulation (the Granger Laws) and cooperatives that bypassed middlemen.
option_explanations.B: Urban immigrant workers were not the Grange's base — they were the constituency of urban labor unions and, later, political machines. The Grange was a farmers' organization rooted in the agricultural Midwest and West.
option_explanations.C: Wealthy industrialists were the Grange's adversaries, not its members. Railroad corporations and grain-elevator monopolies were the powers farmers organized against; industrialists had no reason to join a movement aimed at regulating them.
option_explanations.D: Middle-class corporate managers belonged to the world the Grange opposed. The movement's strength was among producers — farmers squeezed by freight rates, credit costs, and falling crop prices — not among the managerial class of the corporations doing the squeezing.

items.explanation: Farmers faced falling crop prices, high railroad freight rates, expensive credit, and grain-elevator monopolies while corporations amassed unprecedented economic and political power — the grievances that made the Grange a political force.
options: (A) The wave of Irish immigration after the 1840s potato famine.
(B) The concentration of economic power in giant corporations.
(C) The rise of urban political machines.
(D) Corporate campaigns to control markets in Asia and Latin America.
items.stem: The Grange emerged most directly in response to which nineteenth-century development?

option_explanations.A: The Irish famine migration of the 1840s–50s predates the Grange (founded 1867) by a generation and was an urban, eastern phenomenon. The Grange arose among Midwestern and western farmers in the 1860s–70s in response to railroad and credit grievances, not to immigration.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Grange emerged as farmers confronted the concentration of economic power in giant corporations: falling crop prices while railroad freight rates stayed high, expensive credit from eastern lenders, and grain-elevator monopolies controlling storage. Against corporations amassing unprecedented economic and political power, farmers organized for regulation — the Granger Laws — and cooperative enterprise.
option_explanations.C: Urban political machines were a separate phenomenon — city organizations trading services for votes among immigrant workers. The Grange was a rural movement responding to corporate economic power over agriculture, not to city machine politics.
option_explanations.D: Corporate campaigns for markets in Asia and Latin America belong to the imperialism of the 1890s (after the Spanish-American War), decades after the Grange's emergence. The Grange's context was domestic: railroads, elevators, and banks in the 1860s–70s.

items.explanation: The Populist (People's) Party of the 1890s absorbed the Granger program — railroad regulation, an income tax, free coinage of silver, subtreasury farm loans — and carried it into national politics with the 1892 Omaha Platform.
options: (A) The Congress of Industrial Organizations' labor organizing.
(B) The Populist Party's 1890s farmer-labor platform.
(C) The NAACP's civil-rights litigation strategy.
(D) The 1960s New Left student movement.
items.stem: Which later movement most fully carried forward the Grange's political and economic agenda?

option_explanations.A: The Congress of Industrial Organizations was a 1930s industrial-labor movement organizing factory workers — a different century, a different constituency, and a labor rather than agrarian program. It did not inherit the Grange's farmer-focused agenda of railroad regulation and farm credit.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Populist (People's) Party of the 1890s absorbed the Granger program wholesale — railroad regulation, a graduated income tax, free coinage of silver, and the subtreasury plan for farm loans — and carried it into national politics in the 1892 Omaha Platform. Populism was the Grange's political heir.
option_explanations.C: The NAACP's civil-rights litigation strategy addressed racial discrimination through the courts — a different cause, a different method, a different constituency. It carried forward no part of the Grange's agrarian economic agenda.
option_explanations.D: The 1960s New Left was a student movement focused on civil rights, the Vietnam War, and university reform — generationally and programmatically distant from the Grange's farmer politics of railroad rates and farm credit.

items.explanation: Unlike most nativist cartoons of the era, Opper's is sympathetic: it parallels the Pilgrims' seventeenth-century hardships with the gauntlet facing 1880s immigrants — swindling money-changers, baggage thieves, slum landlords, and exploitative employers.
options: (A) The 'new immigrants' of eastern and southern Europe were as dangerous to America as Native peoples had been to the Pilgrims.
(B) America was filling up, and new immigrants would displace native-born Americans just as the Pilgrims displaced Native peoples.
(C) The immigrant stream contained radicals, anarchists, and criminals who threatened the nation.
(D) Newly arrived immigrants faced a gauntlet of exploitation and hardship, just as the Pilgrims had in the 1600s.
items.stem: [Image description: Frederick Burr Opper, 'Just as dangerous now as then,' 1883. A cartoon drawing a parallel between the perils the Pilgrims faced arriving in seventeenth-century America and the perils facing immigrants arriving in the 1880s.] The cartoon's point is which of the following?

option_explanations.A: This misreads the cartoon's sympathy. Opper's cartoon is pro-immigrant: it parallels the Pilgrims' hardships with those of 1880s immigrants to argue that the newcomers deserve the same understanding the Pilgrims receive. It does not portray immigrants as dangerous — that was the nativist position the cartoon answers.
option_explanations.B: The cartoon is not about immigrants displacing native-born Americans. Its parallel runs the other way: just as the Pilgrims faced a gauntlet of perils arriving in the 1600s, so do today's immigrants. The subject is what immigrants endure, not whom they displace.
option_explanations.C: Radicals and anarchists are not the cartoon's subject. Opper shows the gauntlet facing ordinary immigrants — swindling money-changers, baggage thieves, slum landlords, exploitative employers — not a parade of political extremists threatening the nation.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Unusually for its nativist era, Opper's 1883 cartoon is sympathetic: it draws a parallel between the perils the Pilgrims faced arriving in seventeenth-century America and the gauntlet facing immigrants in the 1880s — exploitation by money-changers, thieves, landlords, and employers. The point is that the newcomers' hardships mirror the nation's own founding story and deserve the same respect.

items.explanation: Both the cartoon and the settlement-house movement (Hull House, 1889, founded by Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr) expressed sympathy for immigrants' plight and offered practical aid — a continuity of pro-immigrant sentiment against the era's nativism (Know-Nothings, Palmer Raids, 1924 quotas).
options: (A) Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr founding Hull House (1889) to aid immigrants.
(B) The Know-Nothing Party's 1854 anti-immigrant platform.
(C) Attorney General Palmer's deportation raids during the 1920s Red Scare.
(D) The Johnson-Reed Immigration Act of 1924 establishing discriminatory national-origins quotas.
items.stem: Which of the following best represents a continuity with the sentiment expressed in the Opper cartoon?

option_explanations.A: Correct. Hull House, founded in 1889 by Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr in Chicago, embodied the same pro-immigrant sympathy as Opper's cartoon: settlement workers lived among immigrants, offered English classes, childcare, and practical aid, and advocated for their welfare. Both the cartoon and the settlement-house movement answered the era's nativism with compassion and concrete help — a continuity of sentiment across the 1880s and 1890s.
option_explanations.B: The Know-Nothing platform was the opposite sentiment — organized anti-immigrant, anti-Catholic nativism demanding restrictions on immigrant political power. It represents the hostility Opper's cartoon was pushing back against, not a continuity with it.
option_explanations.C: Palmer's deportation raids during the 1920s Red Scare were state repression of immigrants — rounding up and deporting suspected radicals. That is the nativist tradition at its most coercive, the antithesis of the cartoon's sympathy.
option_explanations.D: The Johnson-Reed Act of 1924 established discriminatory national-origins quotas designed to choke off immigration from southern and eastern Europe and Asia. It is the legislative triumph of the nativism Opper opposed, not a continuation of his pro-immigrant sentiment.

items.explanation: Rice could not match Standard Oil's prices — one to three cents a gallon less — because the railroads were 'in league with' Rockefeller, granting rebates his own Ohio Oil Works never got. This is the predatory mechanism behind horizontal integration: a dominant refiner leveraging transportation deals to price rivals out of the market, then absorbing them.
options: (A) How a dominant firm used secret rebates and special deals to undersell and crush smaller competitors.
(B) The effectiveness of federal regulation in equalizing railroad freight rates.
(C) The benefits of vertical consolidation from oil wells to retail sales.
(D) The decisive role of labor unions in setting oil prices.
items.stem: The advantage Rice describes — railroads quietly charging Standard Oil less than its rivals — best illustrates which of the following?
items.stimulus: "I am but one of many victims of Rockefeller's colossal combination.... I established what was known as the Ohio Oil Works.... I found... that the Standard Oil Company was offering the same quality of oil at much lower prices than I could do — from one to three cents a gallon less than I could possibly sell it for. I sought for the reason and found that the railroads were in league with the Standard Oil concern at every point, giving it discriminating rates and privileges of all kinds as against myself and all outside competitors." — George Rice, 'How I Was Ruined by Rockefeller,' New York World, October 16, 1898

option_explanations.A: Correct. Rice's testimony describes the mechanism precisely: Standard Oil got secret rebates and special deals from the railroads — 'in league with the Standard Oil concern at every point' — letting it sell oil one to three cents a gallon below what an independent refiner like his Ohio Oil Works could possibly charge. Unable to match those prices, smaller competitors were undersold and then absorbed. That is how a dominant firm used transportation deals to crush rivals: the predatory engine of horizontal integration.
option_explanations.B: No effective federal regulation existed when Rice testified. The Interstate Commerce Act (1887) came later and was weak in its early years; the secret rebates Rice describes flourished precisely because freight rates were unregulated. The passage illustrates the absence of regulation, not its effectiveness.
option_explanations.C: Vertical consolidation — controlling everything from wells to retail — was part of Standard Oil's empire, but it is not the advantage Rice describes. His specific complaint is about discriminatory railroad rebates: a horizontal predation mechanism (using transport deals to undersell competing refiners), not about owning the whole supply chain.
option_explanations.D: Labor unions played no role in setting oil prices in Rice's account. The price gap he could not close came from railroad rebates granted to Standard Oil, not from union wage scales or labor action.

items.explanation: Reformers passed the Sherman Antitrust Act (1890), but in U.S. v. E.C. Knight (1895) the Court confined it to interstate 'trade,' exempting manufacturing — leaving the sugar trust (98% of refining) untouched and blunting federal antitrust power for a generation.
options: (A) Congress passed antitrust laws but presidents routinely vetoed them.
(B) Reformers, politicians, and labor leaders quickly succeeded in restructuring the economy.
(C) Most Americans rejected antitrust efforts as communistic and un-American.
(D) Supreme Court rulings narrowed antitrust law, shielding manufacturers from regulation.
items.stem: Efforts to curb corporate power in the 1890s and 1900s were most significantly limited by which of the following?

option_explanations.A: Presidents did not routinely veto antitrust laws — the Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) was signed into law, not vetoed. The limitation came afterward, in how courts interpreted the law, not in presidential vetoes blocking it.
option_explanations.B: This describes a success that never happened. Reformers did not quickly restructure the economy in the 1890s–1900s; the trusts kept growing, and meaningful antitrust enforcement waited for the Progressive Era's later years. The question asks what limited the efforts, and the answer is that they were blunted, not triumphant.
option_explanations.C: Antitrust enjoyed broad popular support in the 1890s — farmers, small businessmen, and labor all demanded action against the trusts. It was not rejected as communistic or un-American; it was one of the era's most popular reform causes. The obstacle was legal, not popular.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The Sherman Act's promise was narrowed by the courts: in United States v. E.C. Knight (1895), the Supreme Court confined 'interstate commerce' to trade as such, exempting manufacturing — so the sugar trust, controlling 98 percent of American refining, escaped untouched. That ruling blunted federal antitrust power for a generation and showed how judicial interpretation could shield the very combinations Congress meant to reach.

items.explanation: Social Darwinism — Herbert Spencer's 'survival of the fittest' applied to society, popularized in the U.S. by William Graham Sumner — taught that great fortunes reflected natural superiority and that regulation would interfere with progress: the standard intellectual defense of laissez-faire industrialism.
options: (A) Herbert Spencer's Social Darwinism, which cast great wealth as fitness.
(B) Henry George's proposal for a single tax on land values.
(C) The Populist Omaha Platform's demands for government intervention.
(D) Upton Sinclair's The Jungle and its expose of the meatpacking industry.
items.stem: Defenders of the corporate practices Rice describes would most likely have appealed to which of the following?

option_explanations.A: Correct. Defenders of Standard Oil's methods appealed to Social Darwinism — Herbert Spencer's 'survival of the fittest' applied to human society, popularized in America by William Graham Sumner. The argument: great fortunes reflect natural fitness, competition weeds out the weak, and government interference with that process would retard progress. It was the era's standard intellectual defense of laissez-faire industrialism and the fortunes it produced.
option_explanations.B: Henry George's single tax on land values was a reformist attack on monopoly and unearned wealth — the opposite of a defense of Standard Oil. George argued that land monopoly, not industrial genius, produced poverty; his followers wanted to tax away precisely the kind of concentrated wealth Rockefeller embodied.
option_explanations.C: The Omaha Platform (1892) demanded government intervention — railroad regulation, an income tax, free silver, the subtreasury — the Populist program against concentrated corporate power. It was the indictment of Standard Oil's world, not its defense.
option_explanations.D: Upton Sinclair's The Jungle (1906) was a muckraking exposé of the meatpacking industry that helped produce the Pure Food and Drug Act — an attack on unregulated corporate practices, not a justification of them. A defender of Rockefeller's rebates would never cite Sinclair.
